newsitem.title: BURUNDI: Burundi slams Tanzania ahead of all-party talks.
newsitem.headline: Burundi slams Tanzania ahead of all-party talks.

text.p: Burundi's government accused Tanzania on Tuesday of driving a decision by regional states to retain sanctions which it said had damaged the peace process.

The accusation came just days before Tanzania hosts all-party peace talks on Burundi aimed at halting the country's civil war, which has left more than 150,000 dead, mostly in massacres, since October 1993.
Tanzania's Foreign Minister Jakaya Kikwete announced on Saturday that regional states would retain sanctions on Burundi until the restoration of democratic rule.
The sanctions were imposed last July after a coup brought retired major Pierre Buyoya to power, but were relaxed in April.

"We regret that for shameful reasons the Tanzanian delegation imposed its own point of view on the other countries to go beyond the (April) decision of the regional heads of state...to ease the suffering of the Burundian people," said a foreign ministry statement.

"We want the national and international community to know that stubbornly holding the Burundian people under the yoke of sanctions is to block irredeemably the peace process and encourage extremists opposed to dialogue."
A senior regional official confirmed Tanzania had led the drive to maintain sanctions.
The Burundian statement also accused Tanzania of favouring Hutu rebel leaders, and of showing this by ejecting government representatives from its embassy in the Tanzanian capital Dar es Salaam.

All-party peace talks due to start next Monday in the northern town of Arusha might see Leonard Nyangoma, leader of the main Hutu rebel National Council for the Defence of Democracy (CNDD) come face to face with government officials.

Ahead of the talks, 80 representatives of political parties, churches and diplomatic missions began a three-day debate on the peace process in Burasira, in Ngozi province, state-run Radio Burundi said.

"Participants will listen to two presentations on the basic principles for the consultation of the nation and the strategies for a common future and an introduction to the conditions for a successful peace process," the radio said.

Tutsi troops murdered Burundi's first freely elected Hutu president, Melchior Ndadaye, in October 1993. The murder sparked a wave of massacres against Tutsis, repression by the Tutsi-dominated army and a civil war.
